transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi, thanks for seeing me. I guess the main thing is… I’ve been having a hard time with tasks that take a lot of focused, sitting-down mental work. Like monthly reports, or planning a bigger health event across multiple sites—things I know are important. I don’t mean to avoid them, exactly, but it kind of feels like I hit a wall, and then I keep putting them off. It’s starting to bother me enough that I thought I should probably talk to someone about it, if that makes sense.
Did you have this same kind of trouble with schoolwork or other sit-down tasks when you were a child?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, I did okay in school, so I don’t want to make it sound worse than it was, but even in elementary school teachers would tell my parents I was bright, just kind of… off in my own world a lot.

I’d lose worksheets, forget about homework, or not turn it in unless my mom went through my backpack every night and made sure it was there. So yes, I guess it was there pretty early, if that’s the kind of thing you mean.
Do you often feel unusually restless or like you have a hard time staying still?

Um… not really, I don’t think. I mean, I can get a little antsy like anybody, especially in long meetings, but I wouldn’t say I’m unusually restless or unable to sit still. That’s not really the main thing I’ve noticed, if that answers it.
Do you notice this same kind of difficulty getting started on boring or effortful tasks in other parts of your life too, like at home?

Yeah, I think so. I don’t want to make it sound like I never do anything at home, because I do, but if something feels like it needs that same kind of sitting-down brain work, I tend to stall.

It’s really the same pattern as with the monthly reports or planning a bigger event across sites. I know it matters, and I’m not trying to ignore it, but I just sort of hit this wall getting started and then I keep putting it off. I’m not sure if that’s what you’re asking, but yes, it does show up outside work too.
When you put off these tasks, is it mainly because you feel anxious or worried about doing them?

Not mainly, no. I mean, I can feel a little stressed once I realize I’ve put it off too long, but the starting point isn’t really fear, exactly.

It’s more like… anything that takes real sitting-down brain work, like the monthly reports or planning something across multiple sites, I just hit this wall. I know it matters, and I know I’m capable of doing it, but I keep avoiding getting started. If that makes sense.
Have you been feeling down or depressed lately?

I don’t think so, not in a major way. I mean, I have days where I feel kind of frustrated or worn out, especially when I’m behind on things, but I wouldn’t say I’ve been depressed exactly.

At least, not that I’ve really noticed. Does that make sense?
Do you often make careless mistakes because your attention drifts, even when you understand the work?

Yeah, that does happen. I wouldn’t say I don’t understand what I’m doing, because usually I do. It’s more like I think I’ve checked it, and then my attention must have skipped over something.

Like I’ll send out a clinic staffing schedule or even a soccer league email, and then someone will point out I had the wrong date, or I left off the location, or missed some detail that seems obvious afterward. It’s embarrassing, because it’s the kind of thing I feel like I should’ve caught before sending it.
Do you often get easily distracted by things going on around you, or by your own thoughts, when you’re trying to focus?

Yeah, I do. I mean, I try not to let it happen, especially in meetings, but it’s pretty easy for me to get pulled off track.

Like if I’m listening to a budget update and someone’s phone vibrates, or there are people talking out in the hallway, I’ll suddenly realize I missed the last few minutes. Or sometimes it’s not even something around me — I’ll think of something I forgot for the soccer league, and then I’m gone for a bit mentally.

I don’t think I’m trying to tune out or anything. It just kind of happens, if that makes sense.
Do you often have trouble staying focused all the way through a task or even during a conversation, even when you’re trying to pay attention?

I’m not totally sure how to answer that. I mean, I try to stay with things, and I don’t want to make it sound worse than it is.

Sometimes I’ll realize I’ve kind of drifted before the end of something, like my mind isn’t fully there the whole time, but I can usually pull myself back. In conversations, I think I follow most of it… though I may miss pieces if it goes on a while.

Is that the kind of thing you mean?
Do you often lose or misplace things you need, like keys, paperwork, your phone, or other important items?

I don’t think that’s a big one for me, honestly. I mean, I’ll set my phone down somewhere and have to look around for it like anyone does, but I can’t say I’m constantly losing important things.

With keys and paperwork, I try to keep them in the same place, so it’s usually manageable. Unless I’m missing something you’re looking for specifically?
Once you get started on a task, do you often have trouble following through and finishing it?

I’m not sure I’d say “often,” exactly. I do try to finish what I start, especially at work, because I know people are counting on me.

There are times where I get started and then it kind of… stalls out, or I have to come back to it later. But I don’t know if that’s more than normal. If there’s a clear deadline, I usually get it done eventually. Is that what you mean by trouble following through?
Have these attention and procrastination problems caused clear problems in your life, like hurting your work performance or creating conflict at home?

I mean… I’m still functioning. I don’t want to make it sound like everything’s falling apart, because it’s not. I’m getting by at work and day to day.

But, yes, there have been some clear problems. Deadlines have slipped, and there have been times coworkers had to kind of cover the gaps for me or help smooth things over. And socially, I’ve had to give those last-minute apology texts to friends more than I’d like to admit.

It’s embarrassing, honestly. I try to keep it from affecting other people, but sometimes it does.
Because of these attention and procrastination problems, have you ever gotten a formal warning or poor performance review at work?

Not a formal warning, no… at least not in the sense of being written up. I’ve had things pointed out to me, though, like missed deadlines or needing other people to step in and help cover something I didn’t get finished on time.

My reviews haven’t been terrible, I’m still getting by, but I can tell it’s affected how people see my reliability sometimes. And I’ve had to apologize last minute to coworkers more than I’d like. I’m not proud of that.
Did these attention and procrastination problems get noticeably worse after a specific stressful life change or event?

Yeah… I think it did get more noticeable after something specific. I don’t want to overstate it, but after my friend died, I ended up taking on more of the league and outreach responsibilities, and that’s when it really started to show more.

That’s been going on for, I guess, about a year and eleven months now. I was managing before, or at least I thought I was, but after that change it became harder to keep up in the same way. Does that make sense?
Before your friend died, were these attention and procrastination problems already causing noticeable problems in your work or daily life?

Yeah… I think so, though probably not as obvious as it got later. I was still getting by at work and in the community, so I don’t want to make it sound like I was failing at everything.

But there were already things slipping through. Deadlines would get closer than they should have, or slip, and sometimes people had to cover gaps for me or help smooth things over. And I’d find myself sending those embarrassing last-minute apology messages to coworkers or friends.

So… yes, there were noticeable problems before, just maybe I was better at minimizing them or patching them up at the time.
Do you often avoid or put off tasks because they require a lot of sustained mental effort?

Yeah… yes, I do. I don’t like admitting that, because I’m not trying to be lazy or careless, but that’s honestly one of the main reasons I’m here.

Anything that takes real sitting-down brain work — like monthly reports, or planning out a multi-site health event — it’s like I hit a wall. I know it matters, and I know I need to do it, but I’ll keep putting it off and telling myself I’ll get to it when I can really focus.

And then, of course, it becomes more stressful because I waited too long. Does that sound like what you mean?
Do you often have trouble organizing tasks or activities?

Yeah… I do, more than I probably like to admit.

I can usually tell myself I’m “keeping track,” but when I’m juggling work projects, the memorial committee things, and outreach events, it gets messy fast. I’ll have notes in three different places, and then I’m not really sure what needs to happen first.

So I end up spending too much time trying to sort it out, and then I’m rushing at the end. I don’t know if that counts as organizing trouble exactly, but… yes, that’s definitely been happening.
Do people often tell you that you seem not to listen when they’re speaking to you directly, even when you’re trying to pay attention?

I’m not totally sure, honestly. I don’t think people say that to me a lot, at least not directly like, “you’re not listening.”

Sometimes someone might repeat themselves or ask if I got what they said, and I feel a little embarrassed because I thought I was following. But I don’t know if that’s happening often enough to call it a pattern.

Is that the kind of thing you mean?
Do you often forget everyday responsibilities, like returning calls, paying bills, or keeping appointments?

Yeah… I mean, I try not to let that happen, but yes, it does.

It’s usually not the big obvious things, more the everyday follow-up stuff. Like I’ll mean to return a call from a volunteer, and then the day gets away from me and I realize later I never did it. Or I’ll forget some small errand connected to an event.

And… once or twice, I’ve had to apologize because a community meeting just completely slipped my mind until someone texted me. I felt pretty bad about that. I don’t know if that’s more than what most people deal with, but it’s happened enough that I notice it.
Do you often interrupt people or blurt things out before they’ve finished speaking?

I don’t think so… not often, anyway.

I mean, I might jump in once in a while if I’m worried I’ll lose the thought, but I don’t think people would describe me as someone who’s constantly interrupting or blurting things out. At least, no one’s really brought that up to me.

If anything, I try pretty hard not to come across that way.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the symptoms include poor organization, which would further distinguish inattentive ADHD from anxiety, adjustment disorder, and depression.
doctor.question: Do you often have trouble organizing tasks or activities?

target_item.name: Organization_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: When I’m juggling work projects, memorial committee stuff, and outreach events, I have notes in three different places and I can’t seem to figure out what needs to happen first, so I end up rushing at the end.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about trouble organizing tasks or activities, which matches this symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I do, more than I probably like to admit.

I can usually tell myself I’m “keeping track,” but when I’m juggling work projects, the memorial committee things, and outreach events, it gets messy fast. I’ll have notes in three different places, and then I’m not really sure what needs to happen first.

So I end up spending too much time trying to sort it out, and then I’m rushing at the end. I don’t know if that counts as organizing trouble exactly, but… yes, that’s definitely been happening.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient also has the symptom of often failing to listen when spoken to directly, which would help confirm ADHD inattentive-type symptom count and separate it from anxiety, adjustment disorder, or depression.
doctor.question: Do people often tell you that you seem not to listen when they’re speaking to you directly, even when you’re trying to pay attention?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about seeming not to listen when spoken to directly, which is a separate inattentive symptom not represented in the provided symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not totally sure, honestly. I don’t think people say that to me a lot, at least not directly like, “you’re not listening.”

Sometimes someone might repeat themselves or ask if I got what they said, and I feel a little embarrassed because I thought I was following. But I don’t know if that’s happening often enough to call it a pattern.

Is that the kind of thing you mean?

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the symptoms include forgetfulness in daily activities, to determine if the patient meets full inattentive ADHD criteria rather than subthreshold/unspecified ADHD.
doctor.question: Do you often forget everyday responsibilities, like returning calls, paying bills, or keeping appointments?

target_item.name: Daily_Activities_Forgetfulness
target_item.manifestation: I’ve been forgetting to return calls from volunteers, missing small errands for events, and once or twice I’ve had to apologize because a community meeting completely slipped my mind until someone texted me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about forgetting everyday responsibilities such as returning calls, paying bills, and keeping appointments, which directly matches this symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I mean, I try not to let that happen, but yes, it does.

It’s usually not the big obvious things, more the everyday follow-up stuff. Like I’ll mean to return a call from a volunteer, and then the day gets away from me and I realize later I never did it. Or I’ll forget some small errand connected to an event.

And… once or twice, I’ve had to apologize because a community meeting just completely slipped my mind until someone texted me. I felt pretty bad about that. I don’t know if that’s more than what most people deal with, but it’s happened enough that I notice it.

inference.note: Added further support for ADHD inattentive symptoms (organization problems, forgetfulness of daily responsibilities), making depressive disorder less likely; removed F32.9.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the patient also has impulsive symptoms to distinguish predominantly inattentive ADHD from other/unspecified ADHD presentations and from anxiety/adjustment-related causes.
doctor.question: Do you often interrupt people or blurt things out before they’ve finished speaking?

target_item.reason: The question is specifically about interrupting others or blurting out answers before someone has finished speaking, which is not covered by the listed symptom profile items. The closest listed item is excessive talking, but that is not the same as interrupting or blurting, so I should not force it.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so… not often, anyway.

I mean, I might jump in once in a while if I’m worried I’ll lose the thought, but I don’t think people would describe me as someone who’s constantly interrupting or blurting things out. At least, no one’s really brought that up to me.

If anything, I try pretty hard not to come across that way.

inference.note: Symptoms meet DSM/ICD threshold for predominantly inattentive ADHD: multiple inattentive symptoms since childhood, across settings, with impairment; hyperactive/impulsive symptoms are largely denied. Anxiety/adjustment features appear secondary and do not better explain the chronic pattern, so F41.9 and F43.2 are ruled out; unspecified/other ADHD codes are narrowed to F90.0.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's main presenting concern
opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a persistent pattern of inattentive symptoms beginning in childhood and continuing into adulthood across multiple settings, with clear functional impact. Confirmed symptoms include careless mistakes, distractibility, avoidance of sustained mental effort, organizational difficulty, forgetfulness, and childhood history of losing worksheets/forgetting homework. Hyperactivity-impulsivity is largely denied, supporting predominantly inattentive ADHD rather than another presentation. Anxiety and depressive explanations were not primary, and symptoms predated the later psychosocial stressor.
